q.q: Which best explains artificial intelligence?
o: Modelling aspects of human intelligence in computers so machines can learn and adapt
Any computer program that carries out instructions faster than a person can
A computer system with enough memory to store all human knowledge
Robots built to look and move like humans in everyday settings
q.why: AI models human intelligence in computer systems so machines can function, learn and adapt like people.

q.q: Which of these is an example of machine learning?
o: An expert system that follows rules written by experts
A calculator that works out square roots
A spam filter that improves as users mark emails as spam
A spreadsheet formula that adds up a column of numbers
q.why: Machine learning learns patterns from data rather than following rules written by people.

q.q: What does cognitive science use AI models for?
o: To translate speech from one language to another
To check that expert system rules are correct
To design faster processors for computer systems
To test ideas about how the human mind processes information
q.why: Cognitive science uses computer models of information processing to test ideas about thinking and learning.

q.q: How does rule-based AI differ from machine learning?
o: Rule-based AI needs a neural network; machine learning needs a knowledge base
Rule-based AI follows rules written by people; machine learning learns patterns from data
Rule-based AI produces text and images; machine learning only gives advice
Rule-based AI learns patterns from data; machine learning follows rules written by people
q.why: Expert systems are rule-based; machine learning improves without being explicitly programmed for each case.

q.q: What is meant by narrow AI?
o: AI that is limited to recognising speech and text in only one language
AI that runs on a single computer rather than across many servers
AI that performs specific tasks but cannot transfer its ability to unrelated tasks
AI that matches or beats human ability across any task it is given
q.why: All AI in use today is narrow; general AI matching humans across any task has not been achieved.

q.q: Number-plate cameras and systems that spot tumours on scans are examples of which area of AI?
o: Natural language processing
Image processing and vision
Robotics
Expert systems
q.why: Image processing and vision recognise objects, faces and text in images.

q.q: Which statement about generative AI is supported by the notes?
o: It is an example of general AI that matches humans at any task
It is a rule-based expert system that writes its own rules
It is built with machine learning and produces text, images and code
It works by passing the Turing test before each answer
q.why: Most modern AI, including generative AI, is built with machine learning.

q.q: Which is a reason given for developing AI?
o: To do tasks that are too fast, large, dangerous or tedious for people
To replace all human expert knowledge with simple fixed rules
To remove the need for people to make any decisions at all
To give computers real feelings and a true understanding of language
q.why: The notes give making machines more capable, supporting human thinking and understanding the mind.

q.q: In the Turing test, how do the participants communicate?
o: By text only, typed and read on a screen
By video call with the cameras on
Face to face across a table
By voice over a telephone link
q.why: Text removes clues from voice or appearance.

q.q: When does a machine pass the Turing test?
o: When it beats the human player at a game
When it answers every question correctly
When the player cannot reliably tell it from the human
When it answers more quickly than the human
q.why: It is a test of indistinguishability, not correctness.

q.q: Which is a valid criticism of the Turing test?
o: It can only be carried out using a robot with a body
It tests imitation of human answers rather than understanding
It measures only how fast a machine can calculate
It needs the player to see both respondents
q.why: A program can sound human without understanding what it says.

q.q: Who are the three participants in the Turing test?
o: A human player, a hidden human respondent and a hidden machine
A human player, a knowledge engineer and a hidden machine
Two hidden machines and a human judge who watches them
A human player, a machine and a panel of expert judges
q.why: The player (interrogator) questions a hidden human and a hidden machine.

q.q: In what year did Alan Turing propose his test?
q.why: Turing proposed the test in 1950; 2014 was the Eugene Goostman event.

q.q: Why was the Turing test significant in defining AI?
o: It defined intelligence by examining how a program works inside
It proved that machines can think and understand like humans
It gave the first practical definition, judging intelligence by behaviour
It showed that machines can never imitate human conversation
q.why: It replaced 'can machines think?' with a measurable test of behaviour and became a benchmark.

q.q: What did critics say about the chatbot Eugene Goostman in 2014?
o: It used a voice that sounded exactly like a teenage boy
It convinced all of the judges, so the test was too easy
Its persona as a 13-year-old excused its mistakes and it was mimicking, not reasoning
It answered every question correctly, which proved it was not human
q.why: It convinced 33% of judges, but critics said the persona hid its errors and it was not reasoning or learning.

q.q: Which type of question most often catches a machine out in the Turing test?
o: One that needs a long calculation to be done
One that needs a large amount of factual recall
One that asks about recent news events
One that needs common sense rather than facts
q.why: Common-sense questions, like the trophy and suitcase example, catch out systems that only match words.

q.q: Which is a weakness of the Turing test's scope?
o: It lets the judge be swayed by the respondents' appearance
It ignores other kinds of intelligence such as vision and movement
It is limited to questions about mathematics and logic
It cannot be run with modern computer systems
q.why: Language covers almost any topic, but other kinds of intelligence are ignored.

q.q: What do the hidden units in a neural network do?
o: Store the training data used to teach the network
Display the network's final answer to the user
Process the signals between the input and output units
Take in data such as pixels from outside the network
q.why: Hidden layers do the processing; input units take in data and output units give the response.

q.q: When does a unit in a neural network fire?
o: When the weighted sum of its inputs is above its threshold
When the sum of its weights is above one
When any one of its inputs is greater than zero
When it receives no input from the previous layer
q.why: Each input is multiplied by its weight, the results are summed and compared with the threshold.

q.q: What is adjusted during backpropagation?
o: The number of input units
The training examples
The number of hidden layers
The weights of the connections
q.why: Weights change a little to reduce the error.

q.q: Inputs 1 and 1 arrive along weights 0.2 and 0.5 at a unit with threshold 0.6. Does it fire?
o: Yes, because the weighted sum is 0.7
No, because the weighted sum is 0.7
Yes, because the weighted sum is 0.5
No, because the weighted sum is 0.1
q.why: 0.2 + 0.5 = 0.7, which is above 0.6.

q.q: Inputs 1 and 0 arrive along weights 0.4 and 0.3 at a unit with threshold 0.5. Does it fire?
o: Yes, because the weighted sum is 0.7
No, because the weighted sum is 0.4
Yes, because the weighted sum is 0.4
No, because the weighted sum is 0.3
q.why: 1 x 0.4 + 0 x 0.3 = 0.4, which is below 0.5.

q.q: Inputs 1, 1 and 1 arrive along weights 0.3, 0.2 and 0.4 at a unit with threshold 0.8. Does it fire?
o: Yes, because the weighted sum is 0.9
No, because the weighted sum is 0.9
No, because the weighted sum is 0.5
Yes, because the weighted sum is 0.7

q.q: What does the weight of a connection in a neural network show?
o: How much data the unit can store
How strongly one unit influences the next
How long the signal takes to arrive
How many units are in the next layer
q.why: A weight is a number showing the strength of influence along the connection.

q.q: In backpropagation, how is the error found?
o: By checking each rule in the knowledge base in turn
By counting how many units fired during the example
By comparing the inputs with the weights of each connection
By comparing the actual output with the output it should have produced
q.why: The difference between actual and intended output is the error, fed backwards to adjust weights.

q.q: In which order is the error fed back through a neural network during backpropagation?
o: Hidden layers first, then outputs, then inputs
Input units first, then each hidden layer, towards the outputs
Output units first, then each hidden layer, towards the inputs
All units at once, in a random order
q.why: Backpropagation feeds the error backwards from the output units towards the input units.

q.q: What does it mean for a neural network to be fully connected?
o: Each unit is linked to every unit in the layers on either side
Every unit fires every time an input arrives
The network is connected to the internet for training
Each unit is linked to every other unit in its own layer
q.why: Units connect to every unit in the neighbouring layers.

q.q: Why is a neural network said to be learned rather than programmed?
o: It is written by a programmer who learns the domain first
It is trained by being given a list of IF THEN rules
It works out its rules from examples rather than being given them
It copies its rules from a human expert's knowledge base
q.why: A neural network is not programmed with rules for the task; it learns them from examples.

q.q: Which component of an expert system holds the facts and rules?
o: Inference engine
User interface
Knowledge base
Explanation facility
q.why: The knowledge base stores the domain knowledge.

q.q: What is the knowledge domain of an expert system?
o: The people who use the system's advice
The database of past users' answers
The server on which the system runs
The narrow field of knowledge it covers
q.why: Expert systems work in one narrow field, such as diagnosing engine faults.

q.q: Why is a WIMP interface usually better than a command line for an expert system used by the public?
o: It removes the need for an inference engine
Users choose from menus and buttons instead of learning commands
It uses less memory and processing power than a command line
It is faster for experienced users and easy to script
q.why: Non-specialists cannot be expected to learn exact commands.

q.q: An exam question names the knowledge base and asks for the two other components of an expert system. Which answer is correct?
o: Knowledge engineer and human expert
User interface and human expert
Inference engine and knowledge engineer
Inference engine and user interface
q.why: Experts and knowledge engineers are people, not components.

q.q: What does the explanation facility of an expert system show?
o: How to install the expert system
Which expert supplied each rule
Which rules led to the conclusion
How long each question took to answer
q.why: The explanation facility shows the chain of rules that produced the advice.

q.q: In an expert system, what does the user give and what does the system return?
o: The user gives advice; the system returns a query
The user gives rules; the system returns facts
The user gives the knowledge base; the system returns rules
The user gives a query; the system returns advice
q.why: The user enters a query such as symptoms; the system returns advice such as a diagnosis.

q.q: What is knowledge acquisition?
o: The inference engine collecting facts from the user's answers
The system learning new rules from its own mistakes
The user searching the knowledge base for advice
Gathering knowledge from human experts to put into the knowledge base
q.why: Knowledge engineers gather knowledge from experts during knowledge acquisition.

q.q: Who is a command line interface best suited to when using an expert system?
o: Patients describing their symptoms
Technicians or developers testing rules
Members of the public seeking advice
Sales staff giving quotes to customers
q.why: Command lines are fast once learned and easy to script, but hard for non-specialists.

q.q: How does a knowledge base differ from an ordinary database of records?
o: It holds only the records of previous users and their answers
It holds no rules, only a list of facts about the domain
It holds the rules that encode expertise; the case facts come from the user
It holds the program code for the inference engine
q.why: The knowledge base is not just records: it holds rules, and the facts about the current case come from the user.

q.q: What does the inference engine do?
o: Interviews the human experts to gather new rules for the system
Draws the screens, menus and buttons that the user sees and clicks
Stores the facts and IF THEN rules gathered from the human experts
Applies the rules in the knowledge base to the user's answers to reach conclusions
q.why: The inference engine is the reasoning part of the system.

q.q: What is heuristic knowledge?
o: Rules of thumb from an expert's experience and intuition
Facts about the domain that all experts agree on
The answers the user gives to the system's questions
Rules derived from logic and textbooks alone
q.why: Heuristics come from experience and need judgement; agreed facts are factual knowledge.

q.q: In forward chaining, what does the inference engine do?
o: Deletes any rules that do not fire for the user's answers
Starts from a goal and looks for facts that would prove it
Asks the expert directly for the answer to the query
Starts from known facts and fires rules until it reaches a conclusion
q.why: Forward chaining is data-driven; backward chaining is goal-driven.

q.q: Which type of reasoning best suits diagnosis questions such as 'is it fault X?'
o: Feedforward
Backpropagation
Backward chaining
Forward chaining
q.why: Backward chaining starts from a hypothesis and looks for the facts to prove it.

q.q: Which is an example of factual knowledge in a car fault expert system?
o: A car with a flat battery will not crank
Engines from this factory tend to fail in cold weather
On this model a whining noise is usually the alternator
A good mechanic checks the cheapest part first
q.why: Factual knowledge is widely agreed; the others are rules of thumb from experience.

q.q: How is knowledge usually stored in the knowledge base?
o: As a table of weighted connections
As a list of past users' queries
As IF condition THEN conclusion rules
As recorded interviews with experts
q.why: Rules of the form IF ... THEN ... ELSE are the usual representation.

q.q: Why is heuristic knowledge important in an expert system?
o: It lets the system learn new rules from each user
It lets the system cope with uncertainty and make experienced judgements
It means the system needs no factual knowledge at all
It guarantees the system's conclusions are always correct
q.why: Heuristics capture what makes an expert an expert: judgement under uncertainty.

q.q: Which verbs best describe the inference engine's role, as examiners expect?
o: Displays menus, accepts clicks, shows icons, opens windows on screen
Stores facts, records rules, saves the answers, prints the reports
Interrogates the knowledge base, poses questions, applies rules, draws inferences
Interviews experts, writes the rules, tests the system, refines it
q.why: These are the verbs examiners look for; the others describe the knowledge base, engineer or interface.

q.q: Which type of reasoning suits monitoring, planning and configuration?
o: Pattern matching
Forward chaining
Fuzzy logic
Backward chaining
q.why: Forward chaining is data-driven: it works from known facts towards a conclusion.

q.q: What is missing from an expert system shell?
o: The user interface
The inference engine
The knowledge acquisition tools
The contents of the knowledge base
q.why: A shell is an expert system without its knowledge.

q.q: Which statement uses fuzzy logic?
o: The chance of rolling a six is 1 in 6
The water is warm to a degree of 0.6
The password entered is correct
The lamp is either on or off
q.why: Fuzzy logic gives a degree of truth between 0 and 1; the dice chance is probability.

q.q: Who obtains the facts and rules from the human experts?
o: The end user
The inference engine
The data controller
The knowledge engineer
q.why: Knowledge acquisition is the knowledge engineer's job.

q.q: Where is fuzzy logic most commonly used?
o: In spreadsheet formulas such as SUM
In email servers sending messages
In control systems such as anti-lock brakes
In SQL queries using WHERE clauses
q.why: Fuzzy logic suits vague, continuous control decisions such as braking and washing machines.

q.q: Why does using a shell save money when building expert systems?
o: A shell does not need a user interface, so it is cheaper to build
One shell can produce many systems without writing a new inference engine each time
A shell needs no knowledge engineer or expert to populate its rules
The shell already contains the knowledge of many experts in every field
q.why: Developers populate and configure the shell with rules and facts for each application.

q.q: How does fuzzy logic differ from Boolean logic?
o: Fuzzy logic uses only true or false; Boolean logic uses degrees of truth
Fuzzy logic gives the chance of an event; Boolean logic gives a degree of truth
Fuzzy logic needs no rules; Boolean logic needs IF THEN rules
Fuzzy logic uses degrees of truth from 0.0 to 1.0; Boolean logic uses only true or false
q.why: Boolean logic is 0 or 1; fuzzy logic handles vague ideas true to a degree.

q.q: How does fuzzy logic differ from probability?
o: Fuzzy logic measures the chance of an event; probability measures how true a statement is
Fuzzy logic uses only 0 or 1; probability uses values between 0 and 1
Fuzzy logic measures how true a vague statement is; probability measures the chance of an event
Fuzzy logic and probability are two names for the same idea
q.why: 'Warm to degree 0.7' is fuzzy; 'chance of an even number is 0.5' is probability.

q.q: What is the role of the human experts when an expert system is built?
o: They describe their facts, rules and rules of thumb, then check the advice
They write the inference engine and design the user interface
They type the rules into the shell using a command line
They use the finished system to replace their own judgement
q.why: The experts are the source of knowledge and later check the system's advice.

q.q: Which rule is written in a fuzzy logic style?
o: IF the brake pedal is pressed THEN apply the brakes
IF the brake temperature is over 300 THEN release the brake
IF the brakes are quite hot THEN ease the pressure a little
IF the wheel locks THEN set the brake flag to true
q.why: Fuzzy rules use vague terms such as quite hot and a little.

q.q: What is the purpose of fuzzy logic in an expert system?
o: To store experts' rules of thumb in the knowledge base
To speed up the inference engine by removing unnecessary rules
To make sure that every rule gives a clear true or false answer
To make the best possible decision from uncertain or incomplete data
q.why: Fuzzy logic imitates human reasoning when data is vague or incomplete.

q.q: Which part of knowledge acquisition is hardest for the knowledge engineer?
o: Typing the agreed facts from textbooks into the system
Installing the shell on the users' computers
Drawing out reasoning that experts find hard to put into words
Choosing the colours for the user interface screens
q.why: Experts' heuristics are often hard for them to express, so the engineer must interview and observe.

q.q: Which is a genuine drawback of an expert system in medicine?
o: It always gives the same advice whatever symptoms are entered
It is not available outside normal surgery working hours
It cannot store rules about more than a few different illnesses
It cannot take account of special circumstances a doctor would notice
q.why: It applies its rules without the doctor's wider judgement of the patient.

q.q: Why is life insurance pricing well suited to an expert system?
o: Insurers have no human experts available to consult on prices
Premiums are exactly the same for every applicant who applies
It needs no personal data from the applicant at all
It is a rule-based calculation on factors such as age and smoking
q.why: Clear rules on age, gender, smoking and health make it a good fit.

q.q: How does a car fault expert system usually get information about the car?
o: By being plugged into the car to read its sensors and run tests
By downloading the car's history from the insurer
By asking the driver to remember when the fault began
By the mechanic typing in the car's registration only
q.why: A direct connection lets the system run automatic tests and identify the fault.

q.q: In which medical situation is an expert system particularly helpful?
o: A doctor faces a rare condition they have never seen
A doctor wants to take full responsibility for every decision
A patient's case depends mostly on their personal circumstances
A patient has a very common illness the doctor treats daily
q.why: Expert systems help with rare conditions, triage, out-of-date knowledge and second opinions.

q.q: Who should make the final decision when a medical expert system suggests a diagnosis?
o: A qualified clinician who knows the patient's history
The knowledge engineer who built the system
The expert system, as it combines many experts' knowledge
The patient, using the system's printed report
q.why: The final decision stays with the clinician, who can weigh circumstances the system cannot.

q.q: Which is a drawback of car fault diagnosis expert systems?
o: They give different answers each time for the same fault
They make diagnosis slower than a mechanic working alone
Each manufacturer's system covers only its own cars
They cannot read the car's sensors directly
q.why: The equipment is expensive and limited to the maker's own cars and known faults.

q.q: Why can an expert system be described as deskilling?
o: It removes the knowledge of the experts once it is built
Users may over-rely on it and lose their own diagnostic skills
It needs users to learn very complex commands
It cannot be updated once the rules are entered
q.why: Over-reliance on the system's advice can erode people's own skills.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of an expert system compared with a human expert?
o: It does not learn from its own mistakes
It gives inconsistent advice from day to day
It tires after giving advice for many hours
It cannot combine knowledge from many experts
q.why: Rules can be updated centrally, but the system does not learn from mistakes as a person does.

q.q: Which is a drawback of using an expert system for life insurance quotes?
o: It cannot use smoking status or health in its rules
Applicants with unusual circumstances may be priced unfairly
Quotes differ for two applicants with identical details
Quotes take much longer than with a human consultant
q.why: Rules handle typical cases well but may miss special circumstances; dishonest answers are also hard to detect.

q.q: Which component converts the voice signal into binary data?
o: Analogue-to-digital converter
Microphone
Speaker
Recognition software
q.why: The ADC in the sound card samples and digitises the analogue signal.

q.q: Which method recognises whole words from a short list of allowed replies?
o: Statistical analysis
Pattern matching
Backpropagation
Parsing
q.why: Pattern matching compares the digitised word with stored patterns, as in automated switchboards.

q.q: What is the main difference between NLP and voice recognition?
o: NLP only works on speech, while voice recognition works on text
NLP decodes speech; voice recognition works out the meaning of language
They are the same technology described in two different ways
Voice recognition decodes speech; NLP works out the meaning of language
q.why: Voice recognition converts sound to words; NLP works out meaning, spoken or written.

q.q: Which NLP step uses surrounding words to decide between meanings of 'bank'?
o: Semantics
Parsing
Morphology
Phonology
q.why: Semantics uses context to fix meaning.

q.q: What does the microphone do in a voice recognition system?
o: Picks up the analogue sound wave of the speaker's voice
Matches the sound against stored word patterns
Converts the sound into binary data for the software
Speaks the system's reply back to the user
q.why: The microphone captures the analogue sound; the ADC digitises it.

q.q: Which method predicts the most likely word using grammar rules and probabilities when the sound is unclear?
o: Part-of-speech tagging
Statistical analysis
Pattern and feature analysis
Pattern matching
q.why: Statistical analysis suits dictation and continuous speech.

q.q: What does a parse tree do in natural language processing?
o: Tags each word with its form, such as noun or verb
Uses the wider context to detect sarcasm and emotion
Splits a sentence into noun and verb phrases to find its structure
Compares the sound of the words with a stored dictionary
q.why: Parsing (syntax) finds the structure; tagging is morphology; context is pragmatics.

q.q: Which area of NLP is still the hardest, dealing with wider context, intent, sarcasm and emotion?
o: Phonology
Pragmatics
Morphology
Semantics
q.why: Pragmatics deals with context and intent, the hardest part.

q.q: In a voice assistant, what is the correct order of steps?
o: Application acts, speech recognition, NLP extracts meaning, reply spoken
NLP extracts meaning, speech recognition, reply spoken, application acts
Speech recognition, application acts, NLP extracts meaning, reply spoken
Speech recognition, NLP extracts meaning, application acts, reply spoken
q.why: Speech becomes text, NLP finds the meaning, the application acts, and a response is spoken.

q.q: Why do many phone voice assistants send speech to the provider's servers?
o: The phone's ADC cannot digitise speech on its own
Phones do not have a microphone good enough to hear speech
Servers are needed to store the user's contacts
Complex recognition models need more processing power than the phone has
q.why: Complex models often run on cloud servers.

q.q: Which is an advantage of voice recognition for a user with limited mobility?
o: It works best in rooms with lots of background noise
It gives an effective way to input without typing
It always understands every accent perfectly
It removes the need for a microphone or headset
q.why: Speech can replace typing and pointing.

q.q: Why does NLP find sarcasm difficult?
o: Sarcastic words are never included in its dictionary
NLP cannot process written text at all
The meaning depends on context and intent, not the literal words
Sarcasm can only be expressed in spoken language
q.why: Pragmatics, the context and intent, is the hardest area.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of voice recognition in an open-plan office?
o: The microphone cannot pick up a quiet voice
It always misspells words that are spoken clearly
It cannot be used with any word-processing software
Background noise causes errors and others can overhear
q.why: Noise causes errors and confidential information can be overheard.

q.q: How does NLP help email services filter spam?
o: It listens to voice messages for unwanted words and phrases
It analyses the meaning of each message's text, not just keywords
It blocks every email that contains a link to a website
It counts the number of emails sent by each sender each day
q.why: Spam filters scan the text for meaning to block unwanted email.

q.q: How is NLP used in algorithmic trading?
o: It answers customers' questions about their accounts at any hour
It reads news and reports to decide whether to buy, sell or hold shares
It turns traders' spoken orders into text for a human to type
It filters spam emails sent to the trading firm
q.why: Trading systems extract information from news and act automatically.

q.q: Which is a privacy concern raised by natural language and voice systems?
o: Systems cannot be used without a webcam
Systems publish users' searches on social media
Users' messages and microphones are analysed
Users must type their passwords aloud
q.why: Analysing users' messages and listening through microphones raises privacy concerns.

q.q: Why might a voice recognition system need training?
o: It cannot work until the user types a sample
It may need to learn a particular user's voice
It must be trained each time it is switched on
It needs the user to learn every command first
q.why: Some systems must be trained to recognise a particular user's voice.

q.q: How does voice recognition help a user with literacy difficulties?
o: It produces accurately spelled text from their speech
It reads their handwriting and corrects it
It translates their speech into another language
It removes the need to communicate at all
q.why: Voice recognition gives accurate spelling for users with literacy difficulties.

q.q: Which part of a robot arm is the tool that carries out the task?
o: End effector
Teach pendant
Controller
Drive
q.why: Grippers, welding torches and spray guns are end effectors.

q.q: Which type of robot drive uses compressed air?
o: Pneumatic
Electric
Hydraulic
Mechanical
q.why: Pneumatic drives use air and are fast; hydraulic drives use fluid and are strong.

q.q: What is the main advantage of off-line robot programming?
o: No sensors are needed because every move is fixed
The operator works close to the robot to guide each movement
The robot can be reprogrammed with little interruption to production
It is only used for spray painting irregular surfaces
q.why: Programs are written away from the production line.

q.q: What do sensors provide to a robot's controller?
o: Feedback about position, force, distance or vision
A hand-held keypad for teaching each movement
The tool fitted to the end of the arm for the task
Power to drive the motors that move the arm's joints
q.why: The controller uses sensor data to decide the next action.

q.q: Which disciplines does robotics combine?
o: Computer science, psychology and linguistics together
Electrical engineering, medicine and building architecture
Mechanical engineering, business economics and law
Computer science, mechanical engineering and electrical engineering
q.why: Robotics combines computer science with mechanical and electrical engineering, plus mathematics.

q.q: What is the controller of a robot arm?
o: The tool on the end of the arm that carries out the task
The hand-held keypad used to teach the robot each movement
The electric motor that moves the arm's joints into position
The computer that coordinates the other parts by running the program
q.why: The controller is the robot's brain.

q.q: How does lead-through programming work?
o: The robot learns the task by watching a video of a worker
An operator moves the arm by hand while joint sensors record its positions
A program is written in a high-level language away from the robot
An operator drives each limb step by step using a keypad
q.why: Lead-through records positions as the arm is guided by hand, then plays them back.

q.q: Which programming method has the operator drive each limb step by step with a hand-held keypad, setting position and speed?
o: Sensor feedback programming
Lead-through
Off-line programming
Teach pendant
q.why: A teach pendant is a keypad used one step at a time; lead-through (walk-through) moves the arm by hand.

q.q: Which type of drive is best when a robot must be very strong?
o: Electric
Pneumatic
Solar
Hydraulic
q.why: Hydraulic drives use fluid and are strong; pneumatic drives are fast.

q.q: Which is part of the definition of an industrial robot?
o: A fixed machine that does one job and cannot be changed
A computer that holds an expert's knowledge
A machine that looks exactly like a human
A reprogrammable manipulator that moves in three or more axes
q.why: An industrial robot is an automatically controlled, reprogrammable manipulator with three or more axes.

q.q: Which is a genuine advantage of robots on a production line?
o: They adapt instantly to any new task
They work continuously to a consistent standard
They never need any maintenance or repairs
They are cheap to buy and install
q.why: Consistency and continuous operation are key benefits; capital cost is a disadvantage.

q.q: Why might a person adapt faster than a robot when a product changes?
o: People can work 24 hours a day without breaks or rest
People never need any training to start a completely new task
A new robot program must be written and tested, which can take a long time
Robots cannot be reprogrammed once they are installed on a line
q.why: Writing and testing a new program can be long and complex, while a person can switch task at once.

q.q: What is the main reason for using robots to explore Mars?
o: They can operate where humans cannot survive, without risking lives
They think and make decisions faster than human astronauts
They are much cheaper to launch than orbiting satellites
They need no power source of any kind to operate there
q.why: Robots survive hostile conditions and keep humans out of danger.

q.q: A robot's program contains a fault. What is the likely effect?
o: The fault repeats on every item until it is found
Only the first item is affected before it stops
The fault has no effect because robots are error-free
The robot corrects the fault itself after a few items
q.why: A robot is only as good as its program, so faults repeat on every item.

q.q: Which benefit of robots is best supported with a reason?
o: Lower costs, because robots are cheap to buy and install on the line
Improved quality, because the robot repeats the same movements exactly every time
Better safety, because robots never break down or need maintenance
Improved quality, because robots are modern and expensive machines
q.why: The second mark needs the reason; the other reasons are vague or untrue.

q.q: Why are robots used to spray paint car bodies?
o: They can choose the colour of each car themselves
They keep workers away from hazardous fumes and give consistent quality
They need no programming for each new car model
They use less paint because they are slower than people
q.why: Robots on car lines give speed, consistent quality and keep hazards away from workers.
